routes.label: Use linear height variation along a regular-hexagon diagonal

question: An architect is building a structure that will place vertical pillars at the vertices of regular hexagon \(ABCDEF,\) which is lying horizontally on the ground. The six pillars will hold up a flat solar panel that will not be parallel to the ground. The heights of pillars at \(A,\) \(B,\) and \(C\) are \(12,\) \(9,\) and \(10\) meters, respectively. What is the height, in meters, of the pillar at \(E?\)
solution:
A flat panel has a useful property: along any ground line, its height changes at a constant rate. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AC\), as in [Figure 1](figures/2021_Fall_AMC_10A_Q17_official_solution_fig1.png). Its panel height is the average of the heights at \(A\) and \(C\), namely \((12+10)/2=11\).

In the regular hexagon, \(B,M,E\) are collinear. If its side length is \(a\), triangle \(BMA\) is a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle with \(BM=a/2\), while the opposite vertices \(B,E\) are \(2a\) apart. Thus \(BE=4BM\).

The height rises from \(9\) at \(B\) to \(11\) at \(M\), a rise of \(2\) over one quarter of \(BE\). Over the entire segment it rises by \(4\cdot2=8\), giving height \(9+8=\boxed{17}\) meters at \(E\), choice D.
